what_it_means_heading: What an attic fan does — and the two kinds people mean
what_it_means_paragraphs: An attic fan pulls superheated air out of your attic so it stops radiating down into your living space and overworking your air conditioner. In a Mid-Atlantic summer, an unvented attic can hit 130 to 150 degrees, and that heat soaks through the ceiling all afternoon and evening. A properly sized, thermostat-controlled attic exhaust fan vents that heat out, which lowers the load on your AC and can take real money off a July electric bill. It also reduces the trapped moisture in winter that leads to mold and rotted sheathing.

Two different things get called an "attic fan," and it's worth knowing which you want. An attic exhaust (or ventilation) fan mounts on the roof or in a gable vent and exhausts hot air straight out of the attic — it runs on a thermostat and you never really interact with it. A whole-house fan is different: it mounts in the ceiling of your top floor and pulls cooler outside air in through open windows and up through the attic, cooling the living space itself on mild evenings. We install and wire both; we'll tell you which one fits your goal — cut the AC load, or cool the rooms.

problems_heading_template: Attic fan situations we handle every week in {city_name}
problems_intro_template: Here are the calls {owner_first_name} gets most often from {city_name} homeowners. If your situation matches one of these, you're in the right place.

problem_cards.title: Adding an attic fan to cut summer cooling costs
problem_cards.body: If your second floor is always hotter than the first and your AC runs all afternoon, a thermostat-controlled attic exhaust fan vents the trapped heat before it soaks into your living space. We size the fan to your attic's square footage, wire it on a safe circuit, and set the thermostat so it runs on heat — not all day.

problem_cards.title: Replacing a noisy, seized, or dead attic fan
problem_cards.body: Old attic fans get loud, vibrate, or stop spinning entirely — and a motor that's seized but still getting power is a genuine fire risk. We remove the old unit, install a new fan in the same opening where possible, and wire it clean. If the old thermostat is the actual failure, we'll catch that instead of selling you a whole fan.

problem_cards.title: Adding a thermostat or humidistat control
problem_cards.body: An attic fan should run on a thermostat (heat) and ideally a humidistat (moisture), not a wall switch you forget about. We install the control so the fan cycles on automatically when the attic gets hot or damp and shuts off when it doesn't need to run — which is what actually saves you money and protects the fan motor.

problem_cards.title: Whole-house fan installation
problem_cards.body: Different animal from an attic exhaust fan: a whole-house fan mounts in the top-floor ceiling and pulls cool evening air through open windows and out the attic, cooling the rooms themselves. It needs a dedicated circuit, the right switch or timer, and an insulated cover for winter. We handle the wiring and controls.

problem_cards.title: Solar attic fan wiring and integration
problem_cards.body: Solar attic fans run off a panel and need no house power for the fan itself — but many homeowners want a thermostat, a backup grid connection, or a hybrid unit wired in. We handle the electrical side so it actually switches the way it's supposed to.

problem_cards.title: Attic fan keeps running or won't turn on
problem_cards.body: A fan that runs nonstop is usually a stuck or miswired thermostat; a fan that won't start can be the motor, the control, or a tripped circuit. We diagnose which one it is instead of guessing — sometimes it's a fifteen-dollar control, not a new fan.

problem_cards.title: Gable-mount vs. roof-mount decision
problem_cards.body: A gable fan mounts in the existing gable vent — no roof penetration, simpler install. A roof-mount fan moves more air but means cutting the roof. We'll tell you which fits your attic and your roofline, and coordinate the roof cut to stay watertight if you go roof-mount.

process_intro_template: When you call {phone_display} or request a quote online, here's what happens.

process_steps.title: A real conversation about your goal
process_steps.body: We pick up. You tell us the problem — a too-hot upstairs, a screaming old fan, or just a high summer bill. We ask about your attic, your vents, and whether you want to cut AC load (attic exhaust fan) or cool the living space (whole-house fan). That tells us which fan and what to bring.

process_steps.title: On-site assessment and written estimate
process_steps.body: We look at the attic, the existing ventilation, the gable vents or roof, and the nearest power. We size the fan to the attic square footage and give you a written estimate before any work starts — the fan, the circuit, the control, and any coordination with a roofer if a roof cut is needed. No surprises on the work day.

process_steps.title: Safe circuit and clean wiring
process_steps.body: We run the fan on a properly sized circuit and make a clean, code-correct connection — important in a hot attic where bad connections fail fast. If your panel can't take another circuit, we tell you up front rather than overloading an existing one.

process_steps.title: Mount and control
process_steps.body: We install the fan in the gable or the roof opening, then wire the thermostat and humidistat so it cycles automatically on heat or moisture. For a whole-house fan, we set the switch or timer and fit the insulated winter cover.

process_steps.title: Test and verify it cycles right
process_steps.body: We confirm the fan runs at the set temperature, shuts off when it should, and isn't fighting your attic insulation or pulling conditioned air out of the house. Then we walk you through the controls so you know how it behaves.

faq_items.question: Does an attic fan really lower my cooling bill?
faq_items.answer_html: It can, meaningfully, in a hot-summer climate like {city_name_with_state}. An unvented attic can reach 130 to 150 degrees, and that heat radiates down through your ceiling and forces your AC to run longer. A properly sized, thermostat-controlled attic exhaust fan vents that heat out before it loads up your living space, which shortens AC run-time on the hottest days. The key words are properly sized and thermostat-controlled — an undersized fan or one wired to run all day won't deliver the savings. We size it to your attic and wire the control so it only runs when it's actually hot. Call {phone_display} and we'll assess your attic.
faq_items.answer_schema: An attic fan can meaningfully lower cooling bills in a hot-summer climate. A properly sized, thermostat-controlled attic exhaust fan vents the heat before it loads the living space, shortening AC run-time. The savings depend on correct sizing and thermostat control; an undersized fan or one running all day will not deliver the benefit.

faq_items.question: What's the difference between an attic fan and a whole-house fan?
faq_items.answer_html: They solve different problems. An attic exhaust fan mounts on the roof or in a gable vent and pushes hot air out of the attic only — it runs on a thermostat, you never touch it, and its job is to take heat load off your AC. A whole-house fan mounts in the ceiling of your top floor and pulls cool outside air in through open windows and up out the attic — it cools the living space itself on mild evenings and can let you skip the AC entirely on a nice night. Whole-house fans move more air, need a dedicated circuit and a winter cover, and cost more. Tell us your goal and we'll tell you which one fits.

Whole-house fans move more air, require a dedicated circuit and a winter cover, and cost more.

faq_items.question: My attic fan is loud or stopped working — repair or replace?
faq_items.answer_html: We diagnose before we recommend. A loud or vibrating fan is sometimes just worn bearings or a loose mount; a fan that won't start can be the motor, the thermostat control, or a tripped circuit. Plenty of times the actual failure is a stuck thermostat, not the fan — which is a small fix, not a replacement. That said, if the motor is seized, replacement is the right call, and a seized motor still getting power is a fire risk worth handling promptly. We find the real cause first and tell you straight whether it's a repair or a replacement.
faq_items.answer_schema: The decision to repair or replace an attic fan depends on the cause. A loud or vibrating fan may have worn bearings or a loose mount; a fan that will not start may have a failed motor, a bad thermostat, or a tripped circuit. Often the failure is the thermostat control, which is a small fix rather than a replacement. If the motor is seized, replacement is warranted, and a seized motor still receiving power is a fire risk. A diagnosis identifies the real cause before recommending repair or replacement.

faq_items.question: Do you install the fan and cut the roof, or just the electrical?
faq_items.answer_html: We handle the electrical side fully — the circuit, the wiring, the thermostat and humidistat, and the fan unit itself — and we install gable-mounted fans completely since those use the existing vent with no roof work. For a roof-mounted fan that needs a new roof penetration, we coordinate the roof cut with a roofer so the roof stays watertight, and we do all the wiring and controls. On a straight replacement of an existing roof fan, we typically reuse the existing opening. We'll tell you up front exactly which trades your specific job needs so there are no gaps.

For a roof-mounted fan needing a new penetration, the electrician coordinates the roof cut with a roofer to keep the roof watertight and does all wiring and controls. A straight replacement of an existing roof fan typically reuses the existing opening.

faq_items.question: How is an attic fan controlled — do I flip a switch?
faq_items.answer_html: Ideally not. The right setup runs the fan on a thermostat so it switches on automatically when the attic crosses a set temperature, and often a humidistat so it also runs to clear winter moisture that would otherwise cause mold and rot. That automatic control is what protects the motor and actually saves you money — a fan on a wall switch you forget to flip does neither. We install and set the control so the fan runs when it should and rests when it shouldn't. Whole-house fans use a switch or timer instead, since you run those on demand on cool evenings.
faq_items.answer_schema: An attic exhaust fan is ideally controlled by a thermostat that switches it on when the attic crosses a set temperature, and often a humidistat that runs it to clear winter moisture and prevent mold and rot. Automatic control protects the motor and saves money, unlike a wall switch that may be forgotten. Whole-house fans instead use a switch or timer because they run on demand on cool evenings.

faq_items.question: How long does attic fan installation take?
faq_items.answer_html: A straight replacement of an existing attic exhaust fan, reusing the opening and circuit, is usually a half-day or less. A new attic exhaust fan install — sizing the fan, running a circuit, mounting in the gable or roof, and wiring the thermostat — typically takes a few hours, longer if a new circuit run through the attic is involved. A whole-house fan is more involved because of the larger unit, the dedicated circuit, and the framing work, so it often runs most of a day. We give you a realistic time estimate with the price before we start.
